source.title: A Little Help Goes a Long Way: Efficient LLM Training by Leveraging Small LMs
source.authors: A. S. Rawat; Veeranjaneyulu Sadhanala; A. Rostamizadeh; Ayan Chakrabarti; Wittawat Jitkrittum; Vladimir Feinberg; Seungyeon Kim; Hrayr Harutyunyan; Nikunj Saunshi; Zachary Nado; Rakesh Shivanna; Sashank J. Reddi; A. Menon; Rohan Anil; Sanjiv Kumar

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study does not test scaling laws, scaling-based extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. Its own held-out loss results compare training methods at fixed model sizes; the scaling-law reference appears in a footnote and is not tested.
record.gate_note: The paper reports held-out log-perplexity for its pre-training methods, but does not vary parameter count, training tokens, or compute to fit or test a scaling law. It also reports downstream scores, but does not test whether those scores are predictable from scale or pre-training loss. The scaling-law statement in the footnote cites other work and is not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study compares knowledge-distillation pre-training methods at two fixed sizes (1.5B, 2.8B) on the Pile. It fits no power law and runs no sweep over parameters, tokens or compute. Scaling laws appear only in a footnote citing Hoffmann et al. The 1.5B vs 2.8B and 36K vs 208K checkpoints are two points, not a scaling test. The bounds' dependence on N and NT is theoretical, not an empirical loss law.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors add that SALT reaches Baseline's average few-shot score at about 70% of training steps, saving roughly 28% of wall-clock time. They also present a statistical KD framework with a bias-variance trade-off.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares knowledge-distillation training strategies, not a scaling-law fitting or extrapolation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that outcomes vary with the KD-to-standard-training transition point and transition strategy; these are not tests of scaling-law fit choices.

fits_no_version.finding: At 208K steps, 2.8B models trained with SALT (1.863) and SALTDS (1.857) have slightly lower held-out log-perplexity than Baseline (1.868). RKD has higher log-perplexity (2.071), above even the 1.5B SLM (1.951).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distillation from a smaller teacher early in pre-training can slightly lower a larger model's held-out loss; distilling throughout raises it.

record.problems: The held-out loss comparison uses fixed model sizes and training recipes rather than a sweep across several orders of magnitude; it does not fit or evaluate scaling laws. The table reports no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the retained held-out log-perplexity results. Downstream scores were not recorded because the study does not test their predictability from scale or pre-training loss.

untested.parts: Power-law fall of loss with parameters, tokens or compute; only two sizes and no fit.
Effect of depth, width or other shape choices at fixed parameter count; sizes differ mainly in depth (44 vs 92 layers), and no shape is varied at fixed size.
Other modalities or regimes. SFT results compare methods only, with no scaling law.
Predictability of downstream scores from scale or loss; downstream results are method comparisons only.
Dependence of fitted exponents on setup and fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Footnote §: small LMs are trained beyond the compute-optimal point predicted by Hoffmann et al.; this is a citation, not a test. An appendix shows that a teacher SLM trained about 2.5x longer yields a better student (few-shot average 48.70 vs 47.94). That varies teacher training length, not a scaling law of the student.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law relationships between held-out loss and parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pre-training loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices, and whether curves bend away from a single power law.
